title: How big should your emergency fund be, and where should you keep it?
summary: An emergency fund is the money that stops a job loss or hospital bill from becoming a debt problem. Here is how to size it, where to park it, and how to build it without stalling your investments.
author: RATNESH KUMAR SINGH
content:
Most money plans start with investing. The good ones start one step earlier: with a pile of boring, easy-to-reach money that exists only for bad days. A job loss, a hospital bill that insurance does not fully cover, an urgent family trip, a car repair. Without an emergency fund, each of these gets paid for with a credit card, a personal loan or by selling investments at the worst possible time.

An emergency fund does not make you rich. Its job is to make sure nothing else in your plan has to break when life gets expensive.

How much is enough?

The usual starting point is six months of essential expenses. Not six months of salary: six months of what you must pay to keep the household running.

  • Rent or home loan EMI, and any other EMIs
  • Groceries, utilities, phone and internet
  • School fees and other fixed family costs
  • Insurance premiums due in the next six months
  • Basic transport and medicines

If your essential spending is ₹50,000 a month, six months means ₹3 lakh. Then adjust for your situation:

  • Go higher (9–12 months) if you are the only earner, work in an industry with frequent layoffs, are self-employed or have irregular income, or support parents.
  • You can go a little lower (3–4 months) if both partners earn steady salaries in unrelated fields, and you have good health insurance.

Health emergencies deserve a special mention. An emergency fund is not a substitute for health insurance. A single hospital stay can wipe out months of savings, so a family floater policy should come first, and the emergency fund covers deductibles, exclusions and the gap until a claim is settled.

Where to keep it

An emergency fund has three requirements, in this order: safety, access, and only then returns. You need to get the money within a day or two, and you need all of it to be there. That rules out equity funds and stocks, which can fall 30–40% exactly when a recession costs you your job.

Sensible places, often used together:

  • Savings account: keep about one month of expenses here for instant access, including UPI and card payments at odd hours.
  • Sweep-in fixed deposit: many banks link a fixed deposit to your savings account and break it automatically when your balance runs short. You earn FD interest with near-instant access.
  • Liquid fund: liquid mutual funds invest in very short-term debt and have historically been stable. Redemptions usually reach your bank account the next working day, and many funds offer instant redemption of up to ₹50,000 a day. Gains are taxed at your income tax slab rate.

A simple split for a ₹3 lakh fund: ₹50,000 in savings, ₹1.5 lakh in a sweep-in FD and ₹1 lakh in a liquid fund. Keep it in accounts you can reach without anyone else's signature.

Where not to keep it

  • Equity mutual funds or stocks: too volatile. Emergencies and market crashes often arrive together.
  • Long lock-in products: PPF, NPS, tax-saving FDs and ELSS all have lock-ins or penalties.
  • Gold jewellery: selling or pledging it in a hurry costs making charges and puts you at the mercy of the buyer or lender.
  • Cash at home: a small amount is fine; a large amount earns nothing and is not safe.

How to build it without stopping your investments

Few people can set aside six months of expenses at once. Build it in stages:

  1. First milestone: one month of expenses. This alone covers most car repairs, appliance failures and small medical bills.
  2. Automate it. Set up a standing instruction or SIP into a liquid fund on salary day, so the money leaves before you can spend it.
  3. Use windfalls. Bonuses, tax refunds and gifts can fill the fund much faster than monthly savings.
  4. Split your savings while you build. If you already have SIPs running, you do not have to stop them. Many people split new savings, say 50% to the emergency fund and 50% to investments, until the fund is full.

Using it, and refilling it

Be strict about what counts as an emergency: it is unexpected, necessary and urgent. A sale on a new phone is none of these. A planned holiday or a festival is expected, so it belongs in its own savings goal.

When you do use the fund, make refilling it your first priority before adding to investments again. And review the target once a year: as rent, school fees and EMIs grow, six months of expenses grows with them.

The quiet payoff

The real return on an emergency fund is not its interest rate. It is that your SIPs keep running through a bad patch, your investments never have to be sold at a loss, and you never pay 36–42% a year on a credit card balance to cover a hospital bill. That makes every other part of your plan work better.

title: Term insurance: how much cover do you really need?
summary: Term insurance is the cheapest way to protect a family that depends on your income. A practical way to work out the cover, the policy term, and the mistakes that lead to rejected claims.
author: RATNESH KUMAR SINGH
content:
If anyone depends on your income, term insurance is one of the most important financial products you can buy, and one of the cheapest. It is also one of the most misunderstood. People buy too little cover, buy it too late, or buy an expensive policy that mixes insurance with investment and does both badly.

What term insurance does

A term plan pays a fixed amount, the sum assured, to your nominee if you die during the policy term. If you survive the term, it pays nothing. That is why it is cheap: you are paying only for protection.

Its job is simple. If your income stops, your family should still be able to pay off loans, run the household and meet big goals like your children's education.

Method 1: the income multiple

A common rule of thumb is 10 to 15 times your annual income, plus any outstanding loans. Someone earning ₹12 lakh a year with a ₹30 lakh home loan would look at ₹1.5–2.1 crore of cover.

It is quick and a reasonable floor, but it ignores how many years your family needs support, and what you have already saved.

Method 2: the needs-based calculation

A better way is to add up what your family would actually need, then subtract what is already in place:

  1. Household expenses: annual expenses your family would still have, multiplied by the number of years they would need support, until your youngest child is independent or your spouse retires. Allow for inflation: at 6% inflation, prices roughly triple in 20 years.
  2. Outstanding loans: home loan, car loan and any other debt, so your family keeps the house.
  3. Future goals: children's higher education and weddings, in today's money plus inflation.
  4. Less existing assets: investments your family could use, such as mutual funds, PF and FDs, and any existing life cover.

The gap between what is needed and what exists is the cover to buy. It usually lands in the same range as the income multiple, but you will know why.

How long should the policy run?

Cover your working years, typically until age 60 or 65, or until your youngest child is financially independent and your major loans are repaid. Buying cover until 85 or 99 raises the premium sharply for years when, ideally, your investments should have made insurance unnecessary.

Why buying early matters

Premiums depend mainly on your age and health when you buy, and they stay fixed for the whole term. A healthy 28-year-old pays far less than a 40-year-old for the same cover, and every new health condition can raise the premium or lead to rejection. The best time to buy is when you first have dependants or a large loan.

The mistakes that cause claim problems

  • Hiding information. Declare smoking, alcohol, existing illnesses, family history and hazardous hobbies honestly. Non-disclosure is the most common reason claims are rejected, and it can surface years later.
  • Not telling your family. Your nominee should know the policy exists, which insurer it is with and where the documents are.
  • Relying only on employer cover. Group cover from your job ends when the job ends, which may be when you are older and harder to insure.
  • Choosing only on price. Look at the insurer's claim settlement record and service, not just the cheapest premium.

Don't mix insurance and investment

Endowment plans, money-back policies and many ULIPs combine a small amount of life cover with an investment. The result is usually too little cover and modest returns, with long lock-ins and high costs in the early years. For most people it works better to buy a pure term plan for protection and invest the difference in the premium separately, for example through a SIP in a mutual fund.

Riders worth a look

Riders are add-ons for an extra premium. Useful ones can include accidental death benefit, critical illness cover and a waiver of premium if you become disabled. Read the definitions carefully and compare the cost with buying separate cover.

A quick checklist

  • Cover: needs-based, and at least 10 times annual income plus loans
  • Term: until 60–65, or until your dependants are independent
  • Full, honest disclosure on the proposal form
  • Nominee named, informed and aware of the documents
  • Review cover after marriage, a child, a new loan or a big salary jump

Term insurance is not exciting, and ideally your family never needs it. That is exactly the point.

title: SIP or lump sum? What 20 years of Nifty data actually shows
summary: When you already have the money, investing it at once has usually beaten spreading it out, about 7 times in 10 on Nifty 50 data since 2006. So why do SIPs still make sense for most people?
author: RATNESH KUMAR SINGH
content:
It is one of the most common questions in investing: you have some money to invest, a bonus, an inheritance or savings that have built up. Should you put it all in at once, or spread it out through a SIP or STP (systematic transfer plan) over the next few months?

Instead of opinions, let's look at data. We used the daily NAV history of a Nifty 50 index fund (UTI Nifty 50 Index Fund, regular plan) from 2006 to 2026.

The test

For every month from 2006 onwards, we compared two investors with ₹1.2 lakh:

  • Lump sum: invests all ₹1.2 lakh on the 5th of the starting month.
  • Spread out: invests ₹10,000 on the 5th of each month for 12 months.

Both portfolios were then valued five years after the start. That gave 186 different starting months, through the 2008 crash, the 2020 Covid fall and everything in between.

The result: lump sum won about 7 times in 10

Investing all at once came out ahead in 72% of the 186 periods. In the typical (median) period, the lump sum ended about 5.5% higher than the spread-out investment.

In this test the money waiting to be invested earned nothing. Parked in a liquid fund it would have earned a little, which narrows the gap slightly but does not change the picture. This is not a quirk of Indian data; studies on other markets find the same. The reason is simple: markets rise more often than they fall. Money that waits on the side for months, earning little, usually misses more gains than it saves in losses.

So why do SIPs make sense at all?

Because for most people, this is the wrong question. A salaried investor does not have a lump sum sitting idle. They earn money every month, so investing every month is simply investing as soon as the money arrives. That is exactly what a SIP does.

A SIP's real strengths are behavioural:

  • It removes timing decisions. Nobody has to decide whether today is a good day to invest.
  • It keeps you investing through falls. Automatic purchases continue when headlines are scary, which is when units are cheapest.
  • It builds a habit. Money invested on salary day never gets spent.

What a SIP through a crash looks like

Take someone who started a ₹10,000 monthly SIP in the same Nifty 50 index fund in January 2008, just before the market fell by about 60%:

  • By October 2008: ₹1 lakh invested, worth about ₹77,000.
  • By March 2009: ₹1.5 lakh invested, worth about ₹1 lakh, a paper loss of a third.
  • By December 2010: ₹3.6 lakh invested, worth about ₹4.9 lakh.

The instalments bought during the crash picked up units at very low prices, and those units drove the recovery. The investors who did badly were the ones who stopped their SIPs in early 2009.

When spreading out a lump sum is reasonable

Lump sum wins on average, but not every time, and the losing cases hurt. Someone who invested everything in January 2008 watched it fall by more than half within a year. Spreading a large sum over 6 to 12 months through an STP from a liquid fund can make sense when:

  • the amount is large compared with your existing portfolio, so a bad start would really hurt;
  • you are new to equity, and a big early loss might scare you out of investing for good;
  • you would otherwise not invest at all while waiting for the "right time".

Think of spreading out as insurance against regret. It usually costs a little return, but it can keep you invested, which matters far more.

What the long run looked like

Across 126 different 10-year SIPs of ₹10,000 a month in this fund, the yearly return (XIRR) ranged from about 4.5% to 15.8%, with a median of about 12.3%. The worst result was a SIP that started in April 2010 and was measured in April 2020, right after the Covid crash. Only about 3% of the 10-year periods returned less than 8% a year.

The lesson is not "SIP good, lump sum bad" or the reverse. Invest money as soon as you reasonably can, keep your SIPs running through bad markets, and judge results over long periods. You can test any fund's history with our Fund SIP Calculator, which works on real NAVs.

Based on UTI Nifty 50 Index Fund (regular plan, growth) NAVs from AMFI. Past returns do not guarantee future returns.

title: Step-up SIP: the simple habit that can double your final corpus
summary: Raising your SIP by a fixed percentage every year, in line with your salary, can make a far bigger difference than chasing a better fund. Here is the maths.
author: RATNESH KUMAR SINGH
content:
Most people start a SIP at an amount that felt right in the year they started it, and never touch it again. Five years and three salary hikes later, the same ₹10,000 SIP is a much smaller share of their income. A step-up SIP fixes that by raising the instalment automatically, usually once a year.

What a step-up SIP is

A step-up (or top-up) SIP increases your monthly instalment by a fixed percentage or amount each year. Most fund houses and investment platforms let you set this up when you start the SIP, so it happens without you having to remember.

For example, a ₹10,000 SIP with a 10% annual step-up becomes ₹11,000 a month in year two, ₹12,100 in year three, and so on.

The maths over 20 years

Here is a ₹10,000 monthly SIP for 20 years, assuming a 12% yearly return. The return is for illustration only; real returns will vary.

  • No step-up: you invest ₹24 lakh, and it grows to about ₹92 lakh.
  • 5% step-up each year: you invest about ₹39.7 lakh, and it grows to about ₹1.28 crore.
  • 10% step-up each year: you invest about ₹68.7 lakh, and it grows to about ₹1.86 crore.

A 10% step-up roughly doubles the final amount. No fund choice is likely to add that much: the difference between a good fund and an average one over 20 years is usually far smaller than the difference between investing more and investing the same.

Why it feels painless

A step-up works because it rides on income growth. If your salary rises 8–10% a year, raising your SIP by the same percentage keeps your savings rate constant. Your take-home pay still grows; you simply commit part of every raise before you get used to spending it.

It also counters a hidden problem: inflation. At 6% inflation, ₹1 lakh buys only about ₹31,000 worth of today's goods after 20 years. A SIP that never grows is, in real terms, a SIP that shrinks every year.

How to choose your step-up rate

  • Match your expected salary growth: 5–10% is typical for salaried investors.
  • Start conservatively if unsure: a 5% step-up is easy to sustain and still adds a lot, as the numbers above show.
  • Use a fixed amount if you prefer: some platforms allow a step-up of, say, ₹1,000 a year instead of a percentage.
  • Revisit after big changes: a job switch with a large raise is a good moment for a bigger one-off increase.

Common questions

What if my income falls or I face an emergency? You can usually pause or modify a SIP. The step-up is a plan, not a contract, and it is better to lower it than to stop investing altogether. This is also why an emergency fund matters: it lets your SIP keep running through a bad patch.

Should I step up every SIP? Not necessarily. If you have several SIPs, you can step up the one aligned with your longest goal, such as retirement, and keep the others steady.

Does it matter which month the step-up happens? Very little. Aligning it with your appraisal month makes it easy to remember and afford.

Try it on real data

Our Fund SIP Calculator has a yearly step-up option. Pick any fund, choose a start month and a step-up, and see what the SIP would actually have become on the fund's real NAVs, including the bad years that a fixed-return calculator hides.

The habit is simple: every time your income goes up, let your SIP go up too.

title: XIRR, CAGR and absolute return: which number tells the truth?
summary: Your app shows three different return numbers for the same investment. Here is what absolute return, CAGR and XIRR each mean, and which one to use when.
author: RATNESH KUMAR SINGH
content:
Open any investment app and you will find returns quoted in different ways: "absolute return 86%", "CAGR 12%", "XIRR 12%". They can describe the same investment and still look wildly different. Knowing which is which stops you from being impressed, or disappointed, by the wrong number.

Absolute return: how much it grew, ignoring time

Absolute return is the simplest: the total gain divided by what you put in.

If ₹1 lakh grows to ₹2 lakh, the absolute return is 100%. It does not say whether that took two years or twenty, which is why it is useful only for short periods, usually under a year.

CAGR: the yearly rate for a single investment

Compound annual growth rate (CAGR) answers: what steady yearly return would turn the starting amount into the ending amount over this time?

CAGR = (Ending value ÷ Starting value)1 ÷ years − 1

If ₹1 lakh becomes ₹2 lakh in six years, CAGR = 21/6 − 1 ≈ 12.2% a year. Now the time is built in, so you can compare it with an FD rate or another fund.

CAGR works when there is one investment at the start and one value at the end, such as a lump sum or a fund's NAV growth. Fund factsheets use it for 1, 3, 5 and 10-year returns.

XIRR: the yearly rate when money goes in at different times

A SIP breaks CAGR's assumption. Your first instalment has been invested for ten years, your last for one month. Dividing the gain by the total invested badly understates the return, because much of the money was invested only recently.

XIRR (extended internal rate of return) solves this. It finds the single yearly rate that, applied to every instalment for the exact time it was invested, adds up to your current value. It also handles withdrawals and irregular amounts.

One SIP, two very different numbers

Take a ₹10,000 monthly SIP for 10 years that earned a steady 12% a year:

  • Total invested: ₹12 lakh
  • Value after 10 years: about ₹22.4 lakh
  • Absolute return: about 87%
  • XIRR: 12%

A common mistake is to divide the 87% by 10 and call it "8.7% a year". That is wrong twice over: it ignores compounding and it ignores that most of the money was invested for far less than ten years. The XIRR of 12% is the true yearly rate.

Which to use when

  • Under a year, one investment: absolute return is fine.
  • Lump sum or NAV growth over several years: use CAGR.
  • SIPs, top-ups, withdrawals or your whole portfolio: use XIRR.

Most apps and fund statements show XIRR for your holdings. In a spreadsheet, the XIRR function takes a column of dates and amounts (investments negative, current value positive) and does the work.

Three traps to avoid

  • Comparing SIP XIRR with a fund's quoted CAGR. The fund's 5-year CAGR assumes a lump sum five years ago. Your SIP XIRR over the same five years can be higher or lower depending on the path the market took.
  • Trusting XIRR over very short periods. A 3% gain in two months annualises to an eye-catching number that means little. XIRR is meaningful over a year or more.
  • Forgetting that all these numbers look backwards. A 15% CAGR over the last five years says nothing certain about the next five. Our article on rolling returns explains why a single period's number can mislead.

Our Fund SIP Calculator reports XIRR for SIPs on real NAVs, and Rolling Returns Compare shows CAGR across every holding period in a fund's history.

title: Asset allocation and rebalancing, explained with one simple example
summary: How you split money between equity, debt and gold matters more than which fund you pick. Here is how to choose a mix, and why rebalancing after a crash feels wrong but works.
author: RATNESH KUMAR SINGH
content:
Investors spend hours choosing between two similar equity funds, and minutes deciding how much should be in equity at all. It should be the other way round. How you divide your money between asset classes, your asset allocation, drives most of your portfolio's ups and downs.

The main building blocks

  • Equity (stocks and equity mutual funds): the growth engine. Highest long-term returns, but can fall 30–60% in a bad year.
  • Debt (FDs, PPF, EPF, debt funds, bonds): the stabiliser. Lower returns, much smaller swings.
  • Gold (gold ETFs, gold funds, sovereign gold bonds): a diversifier that has often held up when equity fell, though it has its own long flat spells.
  • Cash: your emergency fund and near-term needs.

Each one behaves differently in different conditions, which is exactly why mixing them works.

How to choose your mix

Three questions decide it:

  1. When do you need the money? Money needed within three years should not be in equity at all. For goals 10 or more years away, equity can take the lead.
  2. How much fall can you live with? Be honest. If a 30% drop would make you sell everything, hold less equity, because a mix you abandon in a crash is worse than a cautious one you stick to.
  3. How stable is your income? A steady salary lets you take more market risk than irregular business income.

A rough starting rule is "100 minus your age" in equity, so 70% equity at 30 and 50% at 50. Treat it as a starting point, not an answer, and adjust using the three questions.

Why the mix drifts

Your allocation does not stay put. Suppose you start with ₹10 lakh split 60% equity (₹6 lakh) and 40% debt (₹4 lakh). Then a crash arrives: equity falls 35% and debt earns 7%.

  • Equity: ₹6 lakh becomes ₹3.9 lakh
  • Debt: ₹4 lakh becomes ₹4.28 lakh
  • Your portfolio is now about 48% equity, not 60%.

In a long bull market the opposite happens: equity grows faster and quietly becomes 75% or 80% of your portfolio, making you far riskier than you planned just when prices are high.

Rebalancing: back to the plan

Rebalancing means moving money to restore your target mix. In the crash example, getting back to 60:40 means moving about ₹1 lakh from debt into equity, buying equity after it has fallen.

That feels wrong. Every headline says markets are falling. But it is exactly the discipline most investors lack: rebalancing forces you to buy what has become cheap and trim what has become expensive, without predicting anything.

When and how to rebalance

  • On a schedule: check once a year, for example on your birthday or in April.
  • On a threshold: rebalance whenever any asset drifts more than 5 percentage points from target, say equity above 65% or below 55% on a 60:40 plan.
  • Use new money first: direct fresh SIPs or bonuses into the underweight asset. This rebalances without selling, which avoids taxes and exit loads.
  • Mind the costs: selling equity funds can trigger capital gains tax and exit loads. Small drifts are not worth fixing.

Change the mix as goals approach

As a goal gets closer, gradually shift its money from equity to debt. For a child's college fee due in 15 years, you might start at 80% equity and move steadily to mostly debt over the last three to five years. A market crash in the final year then cannot derail the goal.

The takeaway

Pick a mix you can stick with through a bad year, write it down, and rebalance when it drifts. It is unexciting, and it is one of the few things in investing entirely within your control. For a look at how gold and equity have behaved together, see our Gold vs Nifty study.

title: How to read a mutual fund factsheet in 10 minutes
summary: Every fund publishes a monthly factsheet packed with numbers. These are the ones that matter, what they tell you, and the ones you can safely skip.
author: RATNESH KUMAR SINGH
content:
Every mutual fund house publishes a factsheet each month: a few pages per scheme full of numbers, ratios and charts. Most investors never open it, and those who do often look only at last year's return. Here is a ten-minute routine that tells you far more.

1. Category and benchmark

Start with what the fund is. SEBI's categories (large cap, mid cap, flexi cap, small cap, ELSS and so on) define what the fund is allowed to own. The benchmark is the index the fund is trying to beat, such as the Nifty 100 for a large-cap fund.

Check that the category fits the role you want the fund to play, and remember that a fund should be compared with its benchmark and its category, not with a hot fund from a different category.

2. Riskometer

SEBI requires every scheme to show a riskometer, ranging from Low to Very High. Most equity funds are "Very High". It is a quick sanity check that the fund matches your risk comfort, but it does not distinguish much between equity funds.

3. Returns versus the benchmark

The factsheet shows returns over 1, 3, 5 and 10 years and since launch, next to the benchmark. Focus on the longer periods and on how the fund did relative to its benchmark. A fund up 30% when its benchmark rose 35% has actually underperformed.

Keep in mind that these are point-to-point returns: they depend heavily on the start and end dates. Rolling returns give a fairer picture of consistency. You can check them for any fund with our Rolling Returns Compare tool.

4. Expense ratio

The expense ratio is the yearly fee, taken out of the fund's assets every day. It is already reflected in the NAV and returns, but it matters because it compounds.

On ₹10 lakh growing for 20 years, a 12% yearly return gives about ₹96.5 lakh. Knock 1% off for fees and the same money grows to about ₹80.6 lakh, a difference of nearly ₹16 lakh. Compare expense ratios between similar funds, and between the direct and regular plans of the same fund.

5. Portfolio: top holdings and sectors

Look at the top 10 holdings and the sector split:

  • Concentration: if the top 10 stocks are 60% or more of the fund, its results depend heavily on a few companies.
  • Overlap: compare holdings across the funds you own. Three large-cap funds holding the same banks and IT companies are not really diversification.
  • Style: a "flexi cap" fund that is almost entirely large caps behaves very differently from one with 40% in mid and small caps.

6. Risk ratios

  • Standard deviation: how much returns swing. Lower means a smoother ride.
  • Beta: how much the fund moves with the market. A beta of 1.1 means it has tended to move about 10% more than its benchmark.
  • Sharpe ratio: return earned per unit of risk. Higher is better, when comparing similar funds.

Use these to compare funds within a category, not across categories.

7. Fund size, turnover and manager

  • AUM (assets under management): very small funds can be unstable; very large small-cap funds may find it harder to buy and sell nimbly.
  • Portfolio turnover: how often holdings change. High turnover means higher trading costs.
  • Fund manager and tenure: a strong 10-year record means less if the manager who built it left last year.

8. Exit load

The exit load is a charge for redeeming within a set period, commonly 1% within a year for equity funds. It matters if you might need the money soon.

What you can skip

The NAV itself tells you nothing about whether a fund is cheap or expensive; a ₹15 NAV fund is not "cheaper" than a ₹150 one. Marketing claims and one-year star performances also deserve little weight.

The 10-minute routine

  1. Category and benchmark: does it fit my plan?
  2. Long-term returns relative to the benchmark
  3. Expense ratio compared with similar funds
  4. Top holdings: concentration and overlap with what I own
  5. Standard deviation and Sharpe ratio against category peers
  6. Manager tenure and exit load

Mutual fund investments are subject to market risks. Read all scheme-related documents carefully.

title: What the Nifty's biggest falls teach long-term investors
summary: A 60% crash in 2008, a 38% fall in 2020 and several smaller drops along the way. What happened to index fund investors in each, how long recovery took, and what it means for your SIP.
author: RATNESH KUMAR SINGH
content:
Every equity investor knows markets can fall. Far fewer know how far, how fast and for how long, and that gap is what turns a normal fall into a panic sale. So let's look at what actually happened to someone holding a Nifty 50 index fund through India's biggest recent falls.

The figures below use daily NAVs of UTI Nifty 50 Index Fund (regular plan, growth), so they are what a real investor experienced, after the fund's costs.

2008: the global financial crisis

The fund's NAV peaked on 8 January 2008 and fell to its low on 27 October 2008: a drop of about 60% in under ten months. ₹10 lakh invested at the peak was worth about ₹4 lakh at the bottom.

Recovery took far longer than the fall. The Nifty index itself climbed back above its 2008 peak in late 2010, but the index fund's NAV, which carries yearly expenses, only got back above its January 2008 level in December 2013, almost six years later.

2015–16: the slow grind

Not every fall is a crash. From its peak in March 2015, the fund slid about 22% to a low in February 2016. There was no single dramatic event, just month after month of losses. It recovered its peak by September 2016. Slow falls like this can be harder to sit through than sharp ones, because there is no obvious moment when the worst is over.

2020: the Covid crash

From 14 January to 23 March 2020, the fund fell about 38% in roughly ten weeks, one of the fastest falls on record. Then came an equally unusual recovery: it was back at its old peak by 9 November 2020, less than eight months after the bottom. Investors who sold in March locked in their losses and often missed the rebound.

2026: the fall we are living through

Falls are not only history. The fund peaked on 2 January 2026 and fell about 15% by 31 March 2026. At the end of September 2026 it was still about 13% below that peak. Nobody knows whether this recovers in months or years, and that uncertainty is exactly what every earlier fall felt like from the inside.

Lesson 1: falls are normal, not rare

Over two decades, a Nifty 50 investor lived through a 60% crash, a 38% crash and several falls of 15–25%. A fall of this size every few years is the price of equity's long-term returns. If you plan for it, it is an inconvenience; if you don't, it is a crisis.

Lesson 2: recovery time varies enormously

Eight months after 2020, nearly six years after 2008. This is why money you need within three to five years does not belong in equity. Nobody can promise which kind of recovery the next fall will bring.

Lesson 3: SIPs turn falls into an advantage

For a SIP investor, a fall means each instalment buys more units. A ₹10,000 monthly SIP started in January 2008 was worth only about ₹1 lakh in March 2009 against ₹1.5 lakh invested. By December 2010, the ₹3.6 lakh invested was worth about ₹4.9 lakh, powered by the units bought cheaply during the crash.

But timing still shows up at the end. Across every 10-year SIP in this fund since 2006, the median yearly return (XIRR) was about 12.3%. The worst, about 4.5%, was a SIP measured in April 2020, straight after the Covid crash. The same SIP looked very different a few months later. What happens near your goal date matters, which is why it pays to move money out of equity gradually as a goal approaches.

Lesson 4: the biggest risk is your own reaction

Each of these falls ended. The investors who lost the most were those who sold near the bottom, stopped their SIPs, or waited for "certainty" before investing again. A written plan, an emergency fund that stops you from being a forced seller, and an asset allocation you can live with protect you better than any market prediction.

Based on UTI Nifty 50 Index Fund (regular plan, growth) NAVs from AMFI. Past returns and recoveries do not guarantee future ones.

title: Index funds vs active funds: what Indian investors should know
summary: Index funds are cheap and predictable; active funds promise to beat the market. How each works, what costs do over 20 years, and where each can make sense in your portfolio.
author: RATNESH KUMAR SINGH
content:
Index funds have gone from a niche product to one of the fastest-growing corners of Indian mutual funds. At the same time, many active fund managers have long records of beating the market. Which deserves your money? The honest answer is "it depends on the job", and understanding how each works makes the choice much easier.

How each type works

An index fund buys every stock in an index, such as the Nifty 50, in the same proportions. There is no stock picking. Its return is the index's return minus its costs and a small tracking difference.

An active fund has a manager and research team choosing which stocks to buy, how much and when, trying to beat a benchmark index. If they succeed, you get more than the market; if they fail, you get less, and you pay a higher fee either way.

Why costs matter so much

Index funds usually charge much less than active funds, especially in their direct plans. The difference compounds every year.

Consider ₹10 lakh invested for 20 years. At a 12% yearly return it grows to about ₹96.5 lakh. If costs take away one percentage point, so the investor earns 11%, the same money grows to about ₹80.6 lakh. That single percentage point costs almost ₹16 lakh. An active fund has to beat the index by more than its extra cost just to break even with the index fund.

What the evidence says

S&P Dow Jones Indices publishes a regular scorecard (SPIVA India) comparing active funds with their benchmarks. Its reports have repeatedly found that most actively managed large-cap funds in India trailed their benchmark over 10-year periods. Large-cap stocks are widely researched, so finding mispriced ones is hard, and the higher fee is a steady headwind.

The picture is more mixed in mid-cap and small-cap funds, where companies are less researched and skilled managers have more room to add value. Even there, results vary widely between funds and over time.

The case for index funds

  • Low cost: more of the market's return stays with you.
  • No manager risk: no star manager to leave, and no style drift.
  • Predictability: you will never badly underperform the market, and you always know what you own.
  • Simplicity: a Nifty 50 or Nifty 100 index fund can be the core of a portfolio for decades.

The case for active funds

  • Room to outperform: a skilled manager can add return, especially in less-researched segments.
  • Flexibility: a manager can avoid overvalued sectors or hold some cash, while an index fund must own whatever is in the index, bubbles included.
  • Broader choice: some strategies, such as focused or value funds, have no simple index equivalent.

A practical middle path: core and satellite

Many investors combine both:

  • Core (60–80% of equity): low-cost index funds covering large caps, such as a Nifty 50 or Nifty 100 fund.
  • Satellite (20–40%): carefully chosen active funds in areas where active management has a better chance, such as mid caps, small caps or flexi cap funds with long, consistent records.

This keeps costs and manager risk low for most of the portfolio while leaving room for outperformance.

How to choose an index fund

  • Tracking error and tracking difference: how closely the fund follows its index. Lower is better.
  • Expense ratio: compare direct plans of funds tracking the same index.
  • Fund size: larger index funds usually track more tightly.

How to judge an active fund

Look at consistency, not last year's return: how often has it beaten its benchmark over rolling 3 and 5-year periods? Our Rolling Returns Compare tool lets you put an active fund next to a Nifty 50 index fund and see how often it actually came out ahead.

title: Good debt vs bad debt: how to use loans without sinking your finances
summary: A home loan can build wealth; a revolving credit card balance can quietly destroy it. How to tell the difference, how much EMI is safe, and which loans to repay first.
author: RATNESH KUMAR SINGH
content:
Debt is neither good nor evil. Used well, a loan lets you buy a home years earlier or pay for an education that raises your income for life. Used badly, it can take a large part of every salary for years. The difference lies in what the loan pays for and what it costs.

What makes debt "good"

Good debt generally has three features:

  • It pays for something that holds or grows in value, or raises your income: a home, an education, a business.
  • It has a reasonable interest rate.
  • Its EMI fits comfortably in your budget.

A home loan is the classic example. But even good debt is expensive. A ₹50 lakh home loan at 8.5% for 20 years has an EMI of about ₹43,391. Over 20 years you pay about ₹54 lakh in interest, more than the amount you borrowed. That is fine if the home fits your life and budget, but it is a strong reason to prepay when you can.

What makes debt "bad"

Bad debt pays for things that lose value or are consumed quickly, often at high interest rates:

  • Credit card balances: unpaid balances typically cost around 3–3.5% a month, or roughly 36–42% a year. ₹1 lakh left unpaid at 3.5% a month grows to about ₹1.5 lakh in a year, before fees and GST.
  • Personal loans for spending: a ₹5 lakh personal loan at 14% for three years costs an EMI of about ₹17,089 and about ₹1.15 lakh in interest, for a holiday or wedding that is over in days.
  • "No-cost" EMIs and buy-now-pay-later: convenient, but they make it easy to commit future income to things you might not have bought with cash.

How much EMI is safe?

A common guideline is to keep all EMIs together under 30–40% of your take-home pay, and lower if your income is irregular. Lenders may approve more, but their limit is what they think you can repay, not what leaves room for savings, insurance and an emergency fund.

Before any new loan, ask: if my income dropped for six months, could I still pay this? If the answer is no, the loan is too big or the emergency fund too small.

Which debt to repay first

If you have several loans and some spare money, the maths is clear: repay the highest interest rate first.

  1. Credit card balances (often 36–42% a year)
  2. Personal loans and consumer loans (typically 12–24%)
  3. Car loans
  4. Education and home loans (usually the cheapest)

Paying off a credit card charging 40% is like earning a guaranteed, tax-free 40% return. No investment reliably offers that, which is why clearing expensive debt usually comes before starting new investments. The exception: keep contributing enough to get any employer match in your provident fund, and keep your emergency fund in place.

Should you prepay your home loan or invest?

This one is genuinely close. Prepaying saves interest at your loan rate, with certainty. Investing in equity has historically earned more over long periods, but with no guarantee. Many people do both: invest regularly through SIPs and use part of each bonus to prepay. If you prepay, ask your lender to reduce the tenure rather than the EMI; it usually saves more interest. Interest on home loans can also bring tax benefits, depending on your tax regime, so factor that in.

Credit cards: use them, don't borrow on them

A credit card paid in full every month is useful: interest-free credit for up to about 50 days, rewards, and a way to build your credit score. The trouble starts only when you pay the "minimum amount due". Set up automatic payment of the full statement balance.

Protect your credit score

Your credit score decides whether you get loans and at what rate. Pay every EMI and card bill on time, keep card usage well below the limit, avoid applying for many loans at once, and check your credit report at least once a year for errors.

The simple rules

  • Borrow for things that grow in value or raise your income, not for lifestyle.
  • Keep total EMIs under 30–40% of take-home pay.
  • Never carry a credit card balance.
  • Repay the most expensive debt first.
  • Keep an emergency fund so a bad month never becomes a new loan.
